## Approach

### Background & Information

This assignment extends practice with JSON and API data with the Nobel Prize API.

### Terminology

-   [**API:**]{.underline} *Application Programming Interface.* Set of rules that allows two softwares to communicate, follow rules, and to share data with each other. In this case, requesting data from a website.

-   [**API Key:**]{.underline} A string of text that acts as a secure passcode for an application to ask a server for the data it is requesting. ***This is not to be shared with anyone!***

-   [**Endpoint:**]{.underline} A specific digital location or web address where a software application can access the digital resources it needs. *Like a library book located in a certain section and we the user want to access and use that book.*

-   [**Request:**]{.underline} The user asking the server if they can extract information without changing anything on the server end.

-   [**Response:**]{.underline} An answer in the form of status codes (200, 400, etc.) from the server to the user. For this definition, getting a response code of 200 means we are permitted to send a request to the server.

### Plan Outline

-   Create requests to the server to extract data

-   Parse from JSON format to use in R tibble

-   Conduct analysis

    -   Creating 4 data-driven questions

    -   Presenting plots or tables to present answers

    -   Interpret the plots and table

## Codebase

### Install Packages

```{r install packages}
# Install packages once if they are missing.
# install.packages(c("httr2", "tidyverse", "jsonlite", "ggplot2", "scales"))
```

### Import Packages

```{r import libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
```

### API Request

Request Parameters

-   [Base URL:]{.underline} `https://api.nobelprize.org`

-   [Endpoint:]{.underline} `/2.1/laureates`

With the Nobel Prize API, an API Key is not required so we can simply request data **without abusing server requests**.

```{r API Request}
url <- "https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates"

req <- request(url) |>
  req_headers(
    `Accept` = "application/json",
    `User-Agent` = "DATA607-week10b-homework"
  )

req
```

#### Request Inspection

```{r request dry run}
req_dry_run(req)
```

#### Performing & Confirming Request

```{r request status}
resp <- req |>
  req_perform()

# Confirm that the server accepted the request.
resp_status(resp)
resp_status_desc(resp)
resp_content_type(resp)
```

### Read Sample JSON Body

```{r parse JSON data}
nobel_prize_JSON <- resp |>
  resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)
 
names(nobel_prize_JSON) 
# we want to investigate laureates

names(nobel_prize_JSON$laureates)
```

This part is where we need to decide what columns we want to keep for our data that we want to analyze, I have selected:

-   `id`

-   `fullName`

-   `gender`

-   `birth`

-   `nobelPrizes`

*Note:* *`nobelPrizes` also contains data inside the variable itself, so we need to further investigate to see what columns we would also want to extract*

#### Investigating `nobelPrize` List

Given that we need to unnest `nobelPrizes`, we need to decide which columns in this new table we have created to keep and to unflatten.

```{r creating first data table}
laureates <- nobel_prize_JSON$laureates

prizes <- laureates |>
  select(id, fullName, gender, birth, nobelPrizes) |>
  unnest(nobelPrizes, names_sep = "_")

glimpse(prizes)
```

```{r flattening data}
prizes_flat <- prizes |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  flatten()

names(prizes_flat)
head(prizes_flat, 3)
```

As we can see we have unflattened the `nobelPrizes` data so now we can see what else is being stored in it more clearly.

As a precaution, we will further unnest the data if needed.

#### Further Unnesting

```{r further unnesting}
prizes_aff <- prizes_flat |>
  as_tibble() |>
  unnest(nobelPrizes_affiliations, keep_empty = TRUE, names_sep = "_") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  jsonlite::flatten() |>
  as_tibble()

glimpse(prizes_aff)

head(prizes_aff)
```

Now we have a data table with clear information of the columns and what we want to extract. Given that this is not the full list of the API data, we will need to start requesting for the full list without abusing the server request.

```{r checking available data counts}
nobel_prize_JSON$meta$offset
nobel_prize_JSON$meta$limit
nobel_prize_JSON$meta$count

# limit of 25
# Offset of 0, meaning the list starts at that very first item
# count of 1028, the total number of items in the dataset
```

### Start Full Data Request

```{r full data request}
total <- nobel_prize_JSON$meta$count 

offsets <- seq(0, total, by = 100) # loop over the offset by 100

pages <- map(offsets, \(off) {
  request("https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates") |>
    req_url_query(limit = 100, offset = off) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)
})

laureates <- map(pages, "laureates") |> bind_rows()
nrow(laureates)
```

`laureates` is our full data that we extracted from the API, now we need to create the table and overwrite our existing `prize_aff`.

```{r unnesting full data}
prizes_aff <- laureates |>
  select(id, fullName, gender, birth, nobelPrizes) |>
  unnest(nobelPrizes, names_sep = "_") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  jsonlite::flatten() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  unnest(nobelPrizes_affiliations, keep_empty = TRUE, names_sep = "_") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  jsonlite::flatten() |>
  as_tibble()

nrow(prizes_aff)
head(prizes_aff, 2)
```

#### Creating the Table

```{r creating table}
nobel_table <- prizes_aff |>
  select(id,
         gender,
         birth_year = birth.year,
         full_name = fullName.en,
         award_year = nobelPrizes_awardYear,
         prize_amt = nobelPrizes_prizeAmount,
         birth_country = birth.place.country.en,
         birth_continent = birth.place.continent.en,
         prize_category = nobelPrizes_category.en
         ) |>
  mutate(
    birth_year = as.integer(birth_year),
    award_year = as.integer(award_year)
  )

glimpse(nobel_table)
head(nobel_table, 3)
```

#### Duplicate Values

```{r checking duplicates}
nobel_prizes <- nobel_table |> distinct()
nrow(nobel_prizes) # There were duplicates
```

#### Missing Values

```{r check for missing values}
colSums(is.na(nobel_prizes))
```

There are around 31-34 missing values, but we can filter it out easily when conducting analysis.

#### Reproducibility Metadata

```{r reproducibility}
retrieved_at <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)

matches_snapshot <- nobel_prizes |>
  mutate(
    retrieved_at = retrieved_at,
    request_url = url,
    .before = 1
  )

head(matches_snapshot,3)
```

### Save to CSV

We want to save this to a CSV file so we can do some offline work with this data.

```{r save to CSV}
write.csv(matches_snapshot, "nobel_table_data_api.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### Read in Data CSV

```{r read in data csv}
data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaiderrX/CUNY-SPS-MSDS/refs/heads/main/DATA607/Week%2010%20-%20Natural%20Language%20Processing/nobel_table_data_api.csv")
```

```{r recreating df without request info}
# Creating a new dataframe where it drops the request information
clean_data <- data |>
  select(-retrieved_at, -request_url)

glimpse(clean_data)
head(clean_data, 3)
```

#### Data Dictionary

|     Variable      |                    Definition                     |
|:-----------------:|:-------------------------------------------------:|
|       `id`        |           Laureate's identifier number            |
|     `gender`      |         Laureate is either male or female         |
|   `birth_year`    |            Birth year of the laureate             |
|    `full_name`    |               Laureate's full name                |
|   `award_year`    |        The year the laureate won the award        |
|    `prize_amt`    | The amount of money laureate gained for the prize |
|  `birth_country`  |            Laureate's country of birth            |
| `birth_continent` |           Laureate's continent of birth           |
| `prize_category`  |     What field/subject the award belonged to      |

: Data Dictionary

### Analysis

For our analysis, we mentioned we want to ask 4 data-driven questions from this dataset.

Upon examining the subset of the data we collected, I would like to inquire the following:

-   [**Question 1:**]{.underline} What is the top country that has won the most Nobel Prizes, and which gender has a higher proportion of that category?

-   [**Question 2:**]{.underline} Per category, what is the average prize amount?

-   [**Question 3:**]{.underline} Per country, are there more males or females winning the Nobel prize?

-   [**Question 4:**]{.underline} Per category, what year had the most winners?

#### Question 1

What categories have won the most Nobel prize, and if possible what is the percentage of the top country and gender that each category contains?

To answer this question, it may be easier to break it up to segments to build up our answer.

```{r question 1 - winner per category}
most_won_categories <- clean_data |>
  count(prize_category, sort = TRUE, name = "total_wins") |>
  mutate(pct_of_all_prizes = round((total_wins / sum(total_wins) * 100), 2))

most_won_categories
```

```{r question 1 - countries portion}
#| eval: false

most_won_categories_country <- clean_data |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_country)) |>
  group_by(prize_category) |>
  count(prize_category, birth_country, sort = TRUE, name = "total_wins") |>
    group_by(birth_country) |>
  mutate(pct_of_country = round((total_wins / sum(total_wins) * 100), 2))

most_won_categories_country
```

```{r question 1 - gender proportion}
#| eval: false

most_won_categories_country_and_gender <- clean_data |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_country), !is.na(gender)) |>
  count(prize_category, birth_country, gender, name = "total_wins") |>
  group_by(prize_category) |>
  mutate(
    category_total = sum(total_wins),
    pct_of_category = round((total_wins / category_total) * 100, 2)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_wins))

most_won_categories_country_and_gender
```

With the initial build idea, we got 277 rows, so we could shorten to top country for each field and compare from there.

```{r}
most_won_categories_country_and_gender <- clean_data |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_country), !is.na(gender)) |>
  count(prize_category, birth_country, gender, name = "total_wins") |>
  group_by(prize_category) |>
  mutate(
    category_total = sum(total_wins),
    pct_of_category = round((total_wins / category_total) * 100, 2)
  ) |>
  top_n(1, total_wins) |> 
  arrange(desc(category_total))

most_won_categories_country_and_gender
```

With our data, we can see almost all of the categories are won by people from the USA and Literature being won by France. The dominant gender is male for all of the categories.

In regard to our data with 277 rows, it was also a male dominant winner in the dataset. Similarly, the USA had the most winners in the categories listed above, but interestingly, the United Kingdom and Germany had he 2nd and 3rd most winners in every category except for Peace and Literature.

#### Question 2

Per category, what is the average prize amount?

```{r question 2}
avg_prize_amt <- clean_data |>
  group_by(prize_category) |>
  summarize(
    total_winner_counts = n(),
    avg_prize = round(mean(prize_amt, na.rm=TRUE), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_prize))

avg_prize_amt
```

Plot

```{r question 2 - ggplot - avg prize}
#| echo: false

ggplot(avg_prize_amt, aes(x = reorder(prize_category, -avg_prize), y = avg_prize, fill=prize_category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Prize Amount Per Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Average Prize Amount",
    fill = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))
```

With the provided table and plot, we can see that Economic Sciences laureates earn the most after being awarded a Nobel Prize, with Literature being the least.

```{r question 2 - ggplot - winner counts}
#| echo: false

ggplot(avg_prize_amt, aes(x = reorder(prize_category, total_winner_counts), y = total_winner_counts, fill = prize_category)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(
    title = "Winner Counts Per Category", 
    x = "Category", 
    y = "Counts", 
    fill = "Category"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

Even though Economic Sciences laureates get more prize amounts, there are less winners versus a category like medicine or physics.

#### Question 3

Per continent, are there more males or females winning the Nobel prize?

```{r question 3}
most_per_continent <- clean_data |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_continent), !is.na(gender)) |>
  count(birth_continent, gender, name = "total_wins") |>
  group_by(birth_continent) |>
  mutate(
    continent_total = sum(total_wins),
    pct_of_continent = round((total_wins / continent_total) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(continent_total), desc(total_wins))

most_per_continent
```

Plot

```{r question 3 - plot}
#| echo: false

ggplot(most_per_continent, aes(x = reorder(birth_continent, continent_total), y = total_wins, fill = gender)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Nobel Prize Gender Breakdown by Birth Continent",
    x = "Birth Continent",
    y = "Total Individual Wins",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("female" = "lightcoral", "male" = "royalblue4"))
```

To refer back to our question 1 for a moment, Europe has more winners than the other continents, but country-wise, the USA has had the most winners.

But in regard to gender, it seems like this is a male dominant data pull where there are less female than male laureates.

#### Question 4

Per category, what year had the most winners?

```{r question 4}
years_most_winner <- clean_data |>
  count(prize_category, award_year, name = "winner_count") |>
  group_by(prize_category) |>
  slice_max(order_by = winner_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

years_most_winner
```

It seems that all of the winners for each category is within the 20th century.

## Conclusion

Working with APIs can be difficult as it is a hassle to get the exact data that we want and going through the long data lists to extract it. Luckily with the Nobel Prize API, it did not need an API key so a bit of the struggle was taken off.

Then after analyzing the data, it was fascinating to me that there was a higher prize in one category than the other. Initially I had thought medicine or physics would be the top category but it had shocked me it was Economic Sciences. Similarly shocking that there are more male than females winning Nobel prizes, but also surprising that Europe has the most winners but in North America, the USA has more winners in 5/6 of the categories. Lastly, it is astonishing that there are not a lot of 21st century winners per category.
